title: Japanese mothers marked a pretend snack with extra smiles, looks, and sounds
summary: In a study of 31 Japanese pairs, mothers smiled more, looked longer, used more sound effects, and did more snack actions when pretending to eat than when really eating.
body: Naoko Nakamichi compared a pretend snack with a real snack. The 31 mothers smiled more often, gazed at their toddlers longer, used sound effects more often, and produced more snack-related actions in the pretend condition. Some of those changes lined up with the toddlers' apparent grasp of the pretense in the moment. The sample is Japanese mother-infant pairs in one study, offered as an extension of earlier US snack studies that this card does not reopen. It shows how a caregiver can flag pretense. It does not say every culture marks play the same way.

sources.title: Maternal behavior modifications during pretense and their long-term effects on toddlers' understanding of pretense
sources.author: Naoko Nakamichi
sources.note: Supports Experiment 1 with 31 Japanese pairs: more smiles, longer toddler-directed gaze, more sound effects, and more snack actions in pretense than in real eating. Peer-reviewed open copy.
